title: A boy of twelve
hookLine: Maha Singh dies and his twelve-year-old son Ranjit Singh inherits the Sukerchakia misl

lines: MAHA SINGH FALLS ILL ON CAMPAIGN.
cards: The chief of the Sukerchakia misl is out on campaign, Sikh histories say, besieging a fort, when he falls ill. He doesn't recover. Maha Singh is dead, and the band he and his father built has no grown man to lead it.
What it has is his son, Ranjit: a boy, twelve years old in the usual telling, who until that day has been somebody's child. Now the riders are looking at him.

teach.h: THE CHIEF'S PLACE PASSES TO HIS SON.
teach.b: A misl was a band of equals around a chief, and the chief's place could pass to his son. That kept the band together. It also meant the son was sometimes very young.
The riders didn't get to pick a seasoned commander; they got the boy they had.
So feel the weight. A boy who should be learning to ride well is suddenly the name on the banner, and every rival chief nearby notices. Some see an opening.
Sikh memory already held stories of the very young carrying great weight. Guru Har Krishan became Guru as a small child, and Sikhs remember him for compassion, tending the sick in Delhi.
The Guru's younger sons, the Sahibzade, stood firm at Sirhind as children.
Ranjit is not a Guru and not a martyr, but the people around him had been raised on the idea that age is not the measure of a person.
And a boy of twelve doesn't lead alone. Sikh histories say others helped hold the reins at first: his mother, his father's trusted men, and the family he was promised into.
That help is a story for a few days from now. For today, see how the young chief begins: with grief, a band waiting for orders, and a name he hasn't grown into yet.
Every later chapter starts here, with a boy standing where his father used to stand.

how: Sikh histories tell of Maha Singh's death and the young Ranjit Singh inheriting the Sukerchakia misl, the start of the story Sikhs remember as the rise of the Maharaja.

practice: Bring to mind someone young who had to grow up fast, a kid looking after younger siblings, a teenager working to help at home, maybe the person you once were.
Find one plain sentence of encouragement an older person could say to them, and keep it simple; Waheguru with each breath out, if you pray.
